gloss: Added to noun or adjective stems to form a masculine noun of the person concerned with a thing
etymology: Beekes suggests Pre-Greek origin.

gloss: Forms feminine nouns, or feminine forms of adjectives (often accented on the ultima)
etymology: Uncertain, but compare Latin -idus (forming adjectives). Furnée and Beekes also consider it a common Pre-Greek suffix, related to -ιτ- (-it-), -ινδ- (-ind-) and -ινθ- (-inth-).

gloss: a male given name, equivalent to English Ajax
etymology: From earlier Αἴϝᾱς (Aíwās) of uncertain further origin; compare Etruscan 𐌀𐌉𐌅𐌀𐌔 (aivas).
The suffix -κύνθος suggests a Pre-Greek origin. Compare other mountain names like Κύνθος (Kúnthos) and Ἀράκυνθος (Arákunthos).

Of obscure origin. Due to the heavy Scythian influence (evidently Strabo and Pliny went as far as to call them a Scythian tribe), Isidore of Seville thought that the name was a Greek corruption of Scythia, calling the names "not that much different...with one letter changed and one removed."
Compare with Μασσαγέται (Massagétai) and Θυσσαγέται (Thussagétai).

gloss: one of the Gigantes; a Gigas
etymology: Uncertain. Possibly Pre-Greek, or perhaps from a Proto-Indo-European *gag-, with cognates including Lithuanian gògas. Compare the morphology of Ancient Greek Ἀκράγᾱς (Akrágās).

gloss: a male given name from Eumaeus
etymology:
Pre-Greek, proposals include:
* From εὐ- (eu-, “good”) + μαίομαι (maíomai, “seek after, seek for”) + -ος (-os).
* From εὐ- (eu-, “good”) + *μαῖος (*maîos, “foster father”) + -ος (-os). Compare μαῖᾰ (maîă, “foster mother”).

gloss: Zakynthos, Zacynthus, Zante (an island of the Ionian Sea, Greece)
etymology:
Pre-Greek (assumed Pelasgian dialect), but Proto-Hellenic *zákuntʰos can be inferred.
Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀼𐀓𐀯𐀍 (za-ku-si-jo).

Cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀽𐁆𐀫 (ze-pu2-ro), pointing to Proto-Hellenic *Dzépʰuros. Probably related to ζόφος (zóphos, “darkness, west”), both occasionally connected to Proto-Indo-European *(h₃)yebʰ- (“to cover > to copulate, to set (of the sun)”) (whence οἴφω (oíphō)), though either the reflex of the laryngeal in οἴφω (oíphō) or its loss from ζεφ- (zeph-) would be unexplained. More likely Pre-Gr
From Aramaic תַדַּי (Ṯaday), of uncertain origin.

gloss: Cabeiri, a group of enigmatic chthonic deities worshipped especially in Samothrace, Lemnos and Boeotia
etymology: Unknown, though unlikely to be related to Sanskrit कुबेर (kubera, “god of riches and treasure”). The root of the name has been suggested to be the same as that in Κάβαρνοι (Kábarnoi, “priests of Demeter”), indicating a Pre-Greek origin.

gloss: Cerberus, the three-headed dog which guards the entrance to Hades
etymology: Disputed. Suggested to be cognate with Sanskrit शबल (śabala), कर्बुर (karbura, “speckled, spotted”), from Late Proto-Indo-European *ḱerbero- (“dappled, spotted”) (perhaps compare Spot as a popular dog's name in English), but—according to Beekes—this equation is phonetically problematic. Instead, Beekes opts for a Pre-Greek origin.

gloss: Name of one of the Cabeiri in Samothrace, son of Kabeiro and Hephaistos.
etymology: From Pre-Greek, potentially identical to Hattic 𒁹𒄩𒊭𒄠𒈪𒇷 (ᵐḫa-ša-am-mi-li /⁠Ḫašammili⁠/), from *Hatˢmilʸ, and potentially related to Κάδμος (Kádmos).

gloss: The indigenous popular class descending from Sicels who lived in Syracuse before the conquest by the Corinthians in 733 BC.
etymology: Uncertain. Variant forms suggest a Pre-Greek origin. It can nonetheless be compared with other Pre-Greek words, such as: κιλλίβας (killíbas), Κιλλικῶν (Killikôn), Κιλλάκτωρ (Killáktōr), Κίλιξ (Kílix). Compare also κῡ́ρῐος (kū́rĭos), as a hypothetical second element of the other two variants.

gloss: Kythira (also spelt Cythera, Kythera or Kithira), one of the seven major Ionian Islands, Greece.
etymology: According to Beekes, stem ending -ηρ implies a Pre-Greek origin (except for -τηρ).

gloss: Cynthus, a mountain in Delos, Cyclades, Greece
etymology: The name's meaning is unknown, but suggestive of Pre-Greek forms.

gloss: Legendary Sican king, ruler of Camicus, whose myth tells that he was protecting Daedalus intent on hiding from the Cretan ruler Minos; this latter will find a violent death in Sicania (present-day Sic
etymology: Likely related to κόκκᾰλος (kókkălos) (or a potential doublet of it, because of the vowel lengthening), a diminutive of κόκκος (kókkos, “grain, seed, kernel”), which leads to Pre-Greek. Compare, for more, the variant forms of κόχλος (kókhlos, “shellfish”).

gloss: Lamia, a fabulous monster said to feed on man's flesh
etymology: According to Beekes, from λαμυρός (lamurós, “avaricious, voracious, coquettish”), a Pre-Greek word probably related to λαιμός (laimós, “throat, gullet”). Others suggest a late Proto-Indo-European stem *lem- (“ghost, nocturnal spirit”) that was ultimately borrowed from a substrate language such as Etruscan or Anatolian. Compare Latin lemures (“ghosts of the departed”).

gloss: one of the Ligures; a Ligurian
etymology:
The name is of uncertain origin. Room suggests an Etruscan, Basque, or other language isolate ethnonym, hinted by the -sc- element found in older Latin forms ligusc*; Compare Latin Vascones and Etruscus.
Imberciadori more recently connects it with Proto-Indo-European *(s)leyg- (“to smear, make smooth”), deriving possessive *(s)lig-wés- / *(s)lig-us- (“bright”) through an internally derived s-stem

gloss: Lydus, legendary first king of Lydia
etymology:
From Lydian [script needed] (*luwdja, “Luwia”), where the Lydians came to live after being driven away by the Phrygians. Here the -d- is result of affrication of proto-Luwian *-j-. Cognate to Hittite 𒆳𒇻𒌑𒄿𒅀 (Luwiya).
The name's ultimate origin is unclear. Beekes suggests that they received the name of the area's original inhabitants (Pre-Greek/substrate), as they were originally called Μαίονες (Maí

gloss: Lycia (a historical region in southwestern Asia Minor, in modern-day Turkey)
etymology: Likely of Anatolian origin, but of uncertain meaning: compare Hittite 𒇻𒊌𒅗𒊑 (“to light up”), and the placename Λυκαονία (Lukaonía) (related to Lukka).
Pre-Greek origin.

gloss: Mormo, a monstrous spectre in Greek mythology, used as a bogey to frighten children
etymology: Unknown. Beekes thinks a Pre-Greek origin is likely. Maybe related to μόρμορος (mórmoros, “fear, panic”). Generally claimed to be connected with Latin formido, although the parallel is dubious. However, see Middle Armenian մորմ (morm, “tarantula”), which possibly comes from the same substrate source.

gloss: Sardinia (an island in the western Mediterranean Sea, now in Italy)
etymology: From its name in a pre-Roman substrate language, *sard, an indigenous name that likely had religious connotations.

Assuming an original meaning "sparkling, flickering", the word has been connected with σείω (seíō, “to shake”), which is compared to a verb "to be excited, sparkle, gleam" in Sanskrit त्विष् (tviṣ, “brilliance, glitter”), त्वेष (tveṣa, “vehement; brilliant”) and especially Avestan 𐬚𐬡𐬌𐬯𐬭𐬀 (θβisra, “glitter”). The basis for the Greek form would then be *tweys-ro- or *twis-ro-. Furnée compares τίριος

gloss: a Sican or Sicanian (one of the Sicani)
etymology: A Proto-Indo-European tribe of uncertain, possibly Ancient Ligurian affiliation, the Sicani's language is the earliest recorded stratum in Sicily. More at Sicani. Also compare Σικελός (Sikelós).

gloss: Chios (an island in the eastern Aegaean Sea)
etymology: Likely to have come from a Pre-Greek language. Related to Κίος or Κέως ("Ceos island").

gloss: kind of hawk mentioned by Aristotle, perhaps the Bonelli's eagle (Aquila fasciata) or the merlin (Falco columbarius)
etymology: Furnée suggests a Pre-Greek origin in view of the variation λ/ρ.

gloss: light of the sun or moon
etymology: The connection with Sanskrit एजति (éjati, “to tremble, shake”) has been rejected. The epithets of Apollo Ἀσγελατας (Asgelatas) and Αἰγλάτας (Aiglátas) are often compared. The epithets are probably from Pre-Greek. According to Beekes, the noun may be of Pre-Greek origin too.

gloss: a diving bird, perhaps the shearwater
etymology: Usually derived from αἴθω (aíthō, “to kindle”), comparing αἰθός (aithós, “sparkling, glowing; dark-coloured”). However, Beekes suggests a Pre-Greek origin of the word, in view of the suffix "-υια", found also in ἄγυια (águia, “street, highway”), ἅρπυια (hárpuia, “harpy”) and κώδυια (kṓduia, “head; bulb”).
According to Beekes, the overall appearance is Pre-Greek.

Traditionally derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₂emǵʰ-w-eh₁-n, from *h₂énǵʰus (“narrow, tight”), and compared in particular to Old Armenian օձիք (ōjikʻ, “collar”), though this is controversial. Beekes tentatively accepts this etymology, but additionally suggests possible Pre-Greek origin; according to him, the -ήν (-ḗn) suffix renders a Pre-Greek source tentatively reconstructed as *ankʷēn.

gloss: gallus, one of the priests of Cybele in Phrygia that typically castrated themselves
etymology: According to Beekes, the word is probably of Anatolian origin, perhaps originally Pre-Greek. He proceeds to compare synonymous κάβηλος (kábēlos) and κάληβος (kálēbos), both found in the lexicon of Hesychius of Alexandria.

gloss: sort of freshwater fish, perhaps a kind of carp
etymology: Furnée compares βάρακος (bárakos, “kind of fish”), a word listed in the lexicon of Hesychius of Alexandria. According to Beekes, the word is of Pre-Greek origin in view of the many variants existing.

gloss: a plant with wonderful medicinal properties
etymology: Depending on the exact medicinal properties possibly related to βᾰ́λλω (bắllō, “to throw; to strike; to tumble”). In Dioskurides it is given as another name of the squirting cucumber. Depending on the exterior appearance it can also be from βαλιός (baliós, “spotted, dappled”), itself suspected to be from Thracian, Illyrian, or Pre-Greek origin. According to Beekes, it's together with βαλαύστιον (b

Generally taken as an haplology from *βαύναυσος, which would be a compound of βαῦνος (baûnos, “furnace”) and αὔω (aúō, “to scoop, light a fire”). However, Beekes disregards this proposal as folk etymology and suggests a Pre-Greek origin, in view also of the suffix -σος found in other words like κόμπασος (kómpasos) and ὄρυξος (óruxos).

Generally taken as an haplology from *βαύναυσος, which would be a compound of βαῦνος (baûnos, “furnace”) and αὔω (aúō, “to scoop, light a fire”). However, Beekes disregards this proposal as folk etymology and suggests a Pre-Greek origin, in view also of the suffix -σος found in other words like κόμπασος (kómpasos) and ὄρυξος (óruxos).

gloss: kind of freshwater fish, perhaps similar to a perch
etymology: Furnée compares βάλαγρος (bálagros, “kind of barb”) and suggests a Pre-Greek origin.

Connected with βάσκειν (báskein, “to slander”), which is probably from βάζω (bázō, “to speak, say”), but might be related to Latin fascinum (“witchcraft; penis”), in which case both would derive from a European substrate language.

gloss: pudendum virile, the genitals of a man
etymology: Furnée compares this word with the adjective ἀβίλλιον (abíllion, “manly, masculine”); according to Beekes, the prothetic vowel would prove a Pre-Greek origin.

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: πυράγρα (purágra, “pair of fire tongs”), δρέπανον (drépanon, “pruning-knife”).
etymology: Furnée suggests a derivation from Asia Minor and compares Svan ბერეჟ (berež, “iron”), Akkadian 𒀭𒁇 (parzillum), Hebrew בַּרְזֶל (barzel, “iron”), Ugaritic 𐎁𐎗𐎏𐎍 (brḏl) and Phoenician 𐤁𐤓𐤆𐤋 (brzl); furthermore Old English bræs (“brass”) and Basque burdin (“iron”). Or, according to Beekes, from Pre-Greek, in view of the geminate consonants.

gloss: coat of skins worn by shepherds or peasants
etymology: Unknown origin. Somehow connected to Proto-Germanic *paidō; according to Beekes, it is borrowed from this Greek word. The same author connects the word with Albanian petk (“coat”), which shares the same root with the addition of a suffix -k-, suggesting a derivation from a common European substrate. Furnée argues for a Pre-Greek origin.

gloss: bath, an area or room where bathing takes place
etymology: According to Beekes all the various attempts to link this word with βάλανος (bálanos, “acorn”) are semantically unconvincing. The same author considers that, given the semantic category and lack of convincing Indo-European cognates, the word must be of Pre-Greek origin. Furnée compares the noun with Old Georgian აბანოჲ (abanoy, “bathroom”).

gloss: rope drawn across the racecourse signalling the starting and finishing point of the course
etymology: According to Beekes of Pre-Greek origin, given the technicality of its meaning and the similar formation in -ῖδ- found in other words, such as κηκίς (kēkís), κνημίς (knēmís) and κρηπίς (krēpís).

gloss: kind of bag, pouch, or purse generally for holding money
etymology: Unknown. According to Beekes the word is perhaps Pre-Greek, in view of the variation -λλ-/-λ-. It has also been connected with Latin follis (“bellows; purse, sack”) by Krahe, suggesting a derivation from an unprecise language of the northern Balkans.

gloss: kind of cake made with flour and honey
etymology: According to Beekes of Pre-Greek origin, in view of the word βασυμνιάτης (basumniátēs, “pastry cook”), which shows a variation -ν-/-μν-.

gloss: kind of flatfish, perhaps the skate or ray
etymology: Beekes suggests a Pre-Greek origin in view of the similarity with βότις (bótis, “kind of fish”), which would display a vowel interchange that is typical of substrate words. In addition, the same author finds the technicality of this ichthyonym a further proof for a Pre-Greek etymology.

gloss: to milk, emulge, to express milk from cows
etymology: According to Beekes, from a Pre-Greek source, in view of the prefix βδ- and the presence of the geminate -λλ. If the gloss βδαλοί (bdaloí, “garfish; varicose veins”) mentioned by Hesychius of Alexandria is really connected to this verb, then this would strengthen the theory of a Pre-Greek origin,

Lewy proposes a Semitic derivation, comparing the word with Aramaic ܒܙܩ̈ܐ (bizqā, “pebble, gravel”). On the other hand, Beekes sustains a Pre-Greek origin for this noun, in view of the suffix "-ακ-" which is typical of substrate words.

Considering Cretan forms (ἀβλοπής (ablopḗs) for ἀβλαβής (ablabḗs) and ἀβλοπία (ablopía) for ἀβλαβεία (ablabeía)) βλαβ- perhaps resulted from βλαπ- by assimilation, but the interchanges α/ο and β/π are typical of Pre-Greek. See also βλάσφημος (blásphēmos), Latin mulcō (“I beat, maltreat”), Sanskrit मृच् (mṛc, “threatening or injury”) and मर्चयति (marcayati, “to hurt, injure”).

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: βδέλλαι (bdéllai, “leeches”).
etymology: Analyzed as a derivation from a stem βλε- found also in καβλέει (kabléei, “to gulp down”) and βλεῖ (bleî, “to collect honey, milk”). According to Beekes, since this stem cannot be of Indo-European origin, the word must be Pre-Greek, which is confirmed by the alternative form.

According to Beekes, probably of Pre-Greek origin and cognate with βλέπω (blépō, “to see, to perceive”). Hamp had suggested Proto-Indo-European *gʷlep- (“to look”), though he offers no extra-Hellenic comparanda for such a root.
According to Beekes, since the word has no etymology, and since the stem formation is strange, it is probably a Pre-Greek word. Nonetheless a Proto-Hellenic reconstruction *gʷlā́kʰōn is possible.

Conventionally connected with Sanskrit मूर्धन् (mūrdhan, “head, top”) and Old English molda (“upper part of the head, crown”) as *μλωθρός (*mlōthrós). However, this does not explain the variation, which points to Proto-Hellenic *gʷ-. Likewise with Frisk’s suggested connections μέλαθρον (mélathron, “ridgepole”) or βλαστάνω (blastánō, “to sprout, grow”). According to Beekes, the variant suggests a P

gloss: vessel in the shape of the frustum of a cone
etymology: According to Beekes, the word is evidently Pre-Greek, because of the alternation -τ-/-ττ-.

gloss: Hesychius' gives the definition as: βάρβαρον (bárbaron, “foreign; barbaric”).
etymology: According to Beekes, from the same Pre-Greek root of βρίκελος (bríkelos, “name of a tragic mask”) and βρύκος (brúkos, “barbarian”).

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: χιτῶνες (khitônes, “tunics”).
etymology: According to Beekes, from the same Pre-Greek of βρύθακες (brúthakes, “silken tunics”).
According to Beekes, the word is clearly connected with βρόξαι (bróxai, “to gulp down, swallow (again)”) and βρόχθος (brókhthos). The nasal infix leads to a Pre-Greek origin.
The variants, together with the prenasalization, prove that this is a Pre-Greek word.
Of unclear origin. An old folk etymology derives the word from βοῦς (boûs, “ox”) + ὤψ (ṓps, “eye”); another folk theory considers the word onomatopoeic for the fish's ability to cry.

gloss: hole, trench or pit dug in the ground
etymology: This word and the synonymous βόθυνος (bóthunos) have been connected with Lithuanian bedù (“sting, dig”), Latin fodiō (“to dig”) and Middle Welsh bedd (“canal”). In order to explain the discrepancy between Greek β- and Latin f-, dissimilation of Proto-Indo-European *bʰodʰ- to Proto-Hellenic *bodʰ- was assumed, or influence of βαθύς (bathús, “deep, profound”). Beekes prefers to derive the word from

According to Beekes, in view of the alternations and the suffix -ιτον, the word is probably Pre-Greek. Compare also βόλιτον (bóliton, “cow dung”). Close to Proto-Albanian *balgā (“dung”) (Albanian bajgë), which may be from the same substratum, but would point to Proto-Indo-European *bolgʷ- if inherited.
Beekes suggests a Pre-Greek origin.
Unknown but perhaps of Pre-Greek origin. Often connected with βότρυς (bótrus, “bunch of grapes”).

gloss: the skin stripped off a hide, leather
etymology: A loanword of unknown, possibly Pre-Greek, origin. Perhaps cognate with Hittite 𒆳𒊭𒀸 (kur-ša-aš); see there for more.

Unknown; a candidate for Pre-Greek origin. Alternatively from Proto-Indo-European *bow-lo-, from an expressive root *bew- (“to swell, bubble; round object”) (compare Latin bulla (“bubble, knob”), Proto-Germanic *pullaz (“round object”)). Compare also Ancient Greek βολβός (bolbós, “bulb”), βουνός (bounós, “hill, mound; clot”) and βουβών (boubṓn, “swelling; groin”), but according to Beekes these can

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: ἀλλαντία (allantía, “sausages”).
etymology: Unknown. Furnée connects the word with γηθυλλίς (gēthullís, “spring onion”) and ἀγαθίς (agathís, “cake made of sesame”), suggesting a Pre-Greek origin.

The entry by Beekes in his Etymological Dictionary of Greek reads (in paraphrase):
"Unknown. According to Belardi, the word is from the Mediterranean substrate."
Compare Italian galestro (“marl”).

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: ἐρέβινθοι (erébinthoi, “chickpeas”).
etymology: From Pre-Greek, in view of the suffix -ινθος and the variant without prenasalization.

Of uncertain origin. Traditionally connected with γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “to perceive, observe”); however, the lengthened -ω- (-ō-) is left unexplained. A newer theory by Hackstein and Vine, supported by De Vaan, derives the word from Proto-Hellenic *ge-gon-s-, a desiderative from a Proto-Indo-European *ǵh₃en- (“to call”), whence also Tocharian A ken- (“to call”) and perhaps Latin gemō (“to sigh, gro

Frequently assumed to be a reduplicated formation, with Beekes concluding it to be Pre-Greek, and seemingly related to ᾰ̓́γλῑς (ắglīs, “clove of garlic”) and γᾰγγλῐ́ον (gănglĭ́on).
Kroonen (2012) suggests an ultimate Akkadian etymology of the word, comparing it to Arabic جَدِيلَة (jadīla, “braid”). He assumes a metathesis from a by-form *γέγλῑς (*géglīs), from which he reconstructs *γέδλῑς (*gédlī

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: ἀσφόδελος (asphódelos, “asphodel”), νάρκισσος (nárkissos, “daffodil”).
etymology: According to Furnée, from Pre-Greek and related to σχέλινος (skhélinos, “wild cypress”).
According to Beekes, related to γέρρον (gérrhon, “anything made of wicker-work”). The variations point to a substrate origin of these words.

Reduplicated formation. It is often connected with grānum (“seed, kernel”) and Old High German kerno (“pit, stone”), which is formally improbable. According to Beekes, the word is rather a Pre-Greek loan.

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: τρύβλιον (trúblion, “cup, bowl”).
etymology: A Semitic origin has been assumed but Beekes doesn't dismiss a derivation from Pre-Greek, comparing the word with γάβενα (gábena) and κάβος (kábos). See also Latin gabata and Byzantine Greek γαβάθα (gabátha).

gloss: encysted tumour on a tendon or aponeurosis
etymology: Unknown. Traditionally derived from Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“round, swollen”), like Latin galla (“oak apple”). However, Beekes suggests a Pre-Greek origin, comparing the word with ᾰ̓́γλῑς (ắglīs, “clove of garlic”), γέλγῑς (gélgīs, “clove of garlic”) and γᾰ́λῐνθοι (gắlĭnthoi, “chickpeas”).

Traditionally derived from a dissimilation of an unattested earlier *γρᾰστήρ (*grăstḗr, “devourer”), from γρᾰ́ω (grắō, “to gnaw, eat”) + -τήρ (-tḗr, agent noun suffix). If so, Sanskrit ग्रस्तर् (grastar, “(astronomy) eclipser (originally "devourer")”) would be an exact cognate; for a semantic parallel to the Sanskrit term, compare Chinese 蝕 /蚀 (shí, “to corrode, eclipse”), which is derived from 食

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: ἀτυχές (atukhés, “unfortunate”).
etymology: According to Beekes, from Pre-Greek, due to the presence of an "-σ-" after a resonant.

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: ἄγριος μῦς (ágrios mûs, literally “field mouse”).
etymology: According to Beekes, the word shows typical Pre-Greek reduplication and prenasalization, for which γίγγλυμος (gínglumos) and γάγγαμον (gángamon) may be compared.

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: μύξα (múxa, “mucus, slime”).
etymology: Unknown. The comparisons with Lithuanian glėmės (“slime”), glẽmės (“slime”) and Albanian ngjomë (“humid, fresh”) are very doubtful. According to Beekes, the word may be Pre-Greek. Compare also λήμη (lḗmē, “sleep, rheum that collects in the corner of the eyes”).

Has been connected with Proto-Germanic *klainiz (“shining”), but Beekes finds this comparison uncertain. It has also been compared with γαλήνη (galḗnē, “calm weather”) and γλαινοί (glainoí, “ornaments of head-bands”). If this hypothesis be true, then the word would be of Pre-Greek origin.
According to Beekes, since the word has no etymology, and since the stem formation is strange, it is probably a Pre-Greek word. Nonetheless a Proto-Hellenic reconstruction *gʷlā́kʰōn is possible.

From Proto-Hellenic *glṓťťā; further etymology uncertain. Per Beekes, perhaps originally “provided with a point”, equivalent to γλῶχες (glôkhes, “beard of corn”) + -ια (-ia), from Proto-Indo-European *glṓgʰs ~ *gl̥gʰós (“point”) (assuming cognacy with Proto-Slavic *glogъ (“thorn, hawthorn”), but the connection is disputed). Alternatively, related to Proto-Germanic *tulgaz (“tongue”), a poetic word

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: νάπαι (nápai, “glen, vale”).
etymology: According to Beekes, from the same Pre-Greek root of γνύθος (gnúthos, “pit, hollow”).

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: νάρκισσος (nárkissos, “narcissus”).
etymology: According to Furnée, from the same Pre-Greek root of κονίλη (konílē, “marjoram”) and γωνώνη (gōnṓnē, “oregano”).

gloss: bag or chest for old clothes
etymology: In origin, the word probably denoted small things of little value. The formation suggests a Pre-Greek origin and perhaps it is connected to γρῦ (grû, “dirt under the nail”). The comparison with Latin grumus (“hillock”) is unconvincing; better, but still doubtful, is that with Old English cruma (“crumb, morsel”).

gloss: creel, trap for fish, fishing basket
etymology: Like γρῖφος (grîphos, “creel; riddle, enigma”), from Pre-Greek, given the variation π/φ. Comparison with Middle High German krēbe (“basket”) and Old Norse kerfi (“bundle”) must therefore be rejected.

gloss: creel, trap for fish, fishing basket
etymology: Like γρῖπος (grîpos, “creel, fishing basket”), from Pre-Greek, given the variation π/φ.

According to Beekes, definitely from Pre-Greek, but compare Sanskrit गर्गर (gárgara, “whirlpool, eddy, churn; water-jar”) and Latin gurges (“whirlpool, eddy”). Compare also κορκόδρυα (korkódrua, “drain”) and κορχυρέα (korkhuréa, “subterranean drain”).

From a pre-Indo-European Pre-Greek substrate; the proto-form was likely something similar to *gaya, which contracted to *gā at a very early date. The names Δημήτηρ (Dēmḗtēr) and Ποσειδῶν (Poseidôn) also Mycenaean Greek 𐀁𐀚𐀯𐀅𐀃𐀚 (e-ne-si-da-o-ne, “earthshaking (epithet of Poseidon)”) point to an alternative form *δᾶ (*dâ).

gloss: to eat, devour, as wild beasts
etymology: From Proto-Hellenic *dapťō. If this verb is formed from a root δαπ-, this may be compared with Latin daps (“banquet, feast”) and perhaps with Tocharian A tāp- (“to consume, eat”), although the Tocharian initial t- is problematic. Further connections have been proposed with Latin damnum (“loss, damage”) and Old Norse tafn (“sacrifice”), as well as Old Armenian տօն (tōn, “festival, celebration”). Al

Unclear. Has been compared with Sanskrit ग्रीवा (grīvā́, “neck”), Proto-Slavic *griva (“mane”) and Latvian grīva (“estuary”), all from Proto-Indo-European *gʷer- (“to swallow”) (see *gʷriHwéh₂ (“throat”)). This suffers from a problematic initial in the Greek form. However, according to Beekes, a much better etymology is offered by taking the word as a formation related to δειράς (deirás), suggesti

gloss: to soften, knead with the hands
etymology: Unknown. Beekes suggests a Pre-Greek origin, if it is indeed related to διφθέρα (diphthéra).
Clearly related to μάκελλα (mákella, “mattock”). Since this word is from Pre-Greek, also δίκελλα (díkella) should be too.

Traditionally derived from a u-stem formation of δικεῖν (dikeîn, “to throw”). Beekes expresses mild doubts about this, but notes that the word is likely Pre-Greek regardless, due to the older form of Mycenaean Greek [script needed] (de-ku-tu-wo-ko (dektuworgos)) demonstrating ε-ι variation in the first vowel. See also δίσκος (dískos, “discus”).

From an unattested *δίκω (*díkō), of uncertain origin:
* Beekes takes the word as Pre-Greek, perhaps because of a lack of a clear Indo-European etymology as well as the related δίκτυον (díktuon, “fishing net”) being difficult to reconcile as Indo-European.
* Brugmann and Gonda connect the word to δείκνῡμῐ (deíknūmĭ, “to point out, display”), which Beekes rejects on semantic grounds.
* Rix derives

gloss: prepared hide, piece of leather; especially as writing material
etymology:
The origin is uncertain, possibly from Proto-Hellenic *dipʰtʰérā. Related to διψάρα (dipsára, “writing-tablet; piece of leather”) and Mycenaean Greek 𐀇𐁇𐀨 (di-pte-ra).
Since de Saussure, connected with δέφω (déphō) or δέψω (dépsō, “to soften (with the hand)”). Beekes argues that this connection and the alternation between φ (ph) and ψ (ps) point to a Pre-Greek origin.
Compare also Old Persian 𐎮𐎡𐎱𐎡

gloss: to make to run, set in quick motion; to pursue a person, to chase, hunt
etymology: Beekes claims it is of Pre-Greek origin. Probably from δίω.
Probably of Pre-Greek origin.
According to Beekes, of Pre-Greek origin.

gloss: to tear, strip, lacerate, especially in mourning
etymology: Expressive form, usually connected with δέρω (dérō, “to skin, flay”) and δρέπω (drépō, “to pluck, cut off”). However, the word was hardly reshaped after θρύπτω (thrúptō, “to shatter”). The variant δρυφ- and δρυψ- clearly point to a Pre-Greek word, according to Beekes.

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos, “man”).
etymology: Thought to be a compound *νρ-ώψ (*nr-ṓps, “with manly face”) from ἀνήρ (anḗr, “man”), but the absence of ἀ- (a-) is strange. According to Latte, it is a creation of the grammarians. Kuiper accepts the gloss as Pre-Greek, explaining ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos) as arising through prenasalization and prothetic vowel. Pisani considers this word Macedonian and connects it to τρέφω (tréphō, “to breed, bring up

gloss: riverside pasture or water meadow, lowland
etymology: According to Beekes, the word is Pre-Greek in view of the variations.

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: γογγυλίδες (gongulídes, “turnips”) or κολοκύνται (kolokúntai, “gourds”).
etymology: Unknown. Furnée compares θικέλιον (thikélion, “turnip”) and believes the word is Pre-Greek.

gloss: soup or sauce to eat with meat or fish
etymology: Of unclear origin. Generally connected with ζύμη (zúmē, “leaven, beer yeast”), but the ablaut required (ō(u) : ū) is improbable. Connection with ζέω (zéō, “to ferment”) presupposes that Proto-Indo-European *yos-mo- developed into this word regularly.

According to Beekes, a Pre-Greek substrate borrowing tentatively reconstructed as *talakʸa; the element "-σσ-", as well as the local geographic meaning, points to a Pre-Greek origin. Compare the possible cognate Luwian 𒀀𒆷𒀸𒊭𒄠𒈪𒅖 (/⁠alassammis⁠/).
Older theories related the word to ἅλς (háls, “salt”), cf. Latin sāl (“salt”), salum (“sea”), Salacia (“sea goddess”).
Related to θαλυκρός (thalukrós, “warm, glowing”), from Proto-Hellenic *tʰal-ukʷ-, likely of Pre-Greek origin. The connection with θάλλω (thállō, “make green”) is unlikely.

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: οἰκτρόν (oiktrón, “pitiable”), ἥσυχον (hḗsukhon, “quiet”).
etymology: Unexplained. However, Furnée thinks this is a Pre-Greek word, due to suffix -εμος.

gloss: companion of lower rank, comrade, attendant, aide
etymology: According to Beekes, from the same Pre-Greek root as τέραμνον (téramnon, “chamber”).

gloss: to die; (aorist and perfect) to be dead
etymology:
From a root *θ(ᾰ)ν (*th(ă)n) of disputed origin:
* Traditionally compared to Sanskrit अध्वनीत् (á-dhvanī-t, “he disappeared”), ध्वान्त (dhvān-tá-, “dark”), from a Proto-Indo-European *dʰwenh₂- (“to die”). However, Beekes doubts this, on the basis of the zero-grade forms, which would then be *θυνεῖν (*thuneîn), *θύνατος (*thúnatos).
* LIV² reconstructs Proto-Indo-European *dʰn̥h₂-sḱé-, from Proto-I

Unknown; often compared with the second element of Middle Irish gairb-driuch (“bristle”) and Lithuanian drikà (“threads hanging from the loom”), though Beekes rejects both connections and leaves the origin open, noting that the semantic roots used to express the concept of "hair" vary significantly across Indo-European branches. Alternatively Pre-Greek (though Beekes surprisingly does not posit su

gloss: topmost course of stones in a wall, cornice, coping, frieze
etymology: According to Beekes, the word is undoubtedly from Pre-Greek.
The suffix -ίς occurs mostly with plants and birds, so the word is probably Pre-Greek.
Furnée compares the word with τρόνα (tróna, “statues; colorful stitchings”), which proves Pre-Greek origin.

Traditionally derived from Proto-Indo-European *dʰer- (“to hold”), but this root presents a number of problems, such as the lack of the suffix *-onos in Proto-Indo-European, the lack of any words meaning "chair" from this root in any other Indo-European languages, and the lack of any definite Greek descendants from the root itself. Comparisons to θρᾶνος (thrânos, “bench”) and θρῆνυς (thrênus, “foo

This verb may derive from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrewb- (“to crumble, grind”) and is compared to Latvian drubaža (“piece, fragment”), Proto-Slavic *drybati (“to scratch, scrumple”), Proto-Germanic *drupô (“drop”) and Old Irish drúcht (“dew”). It is probable that δρύπτω (drúptō, “to tear, strip”) was modelled on this verb. According to Beekes, it is probably a non-Indo-European substrate word.

This word is often connected with θρόνος (thrónos, “throne”), together with θρῆνυς (thrênus, “footstool”). Recently, De Lamberterie has argued that θρόνος (thrónos) is a younger form of *θόρνος (*thórnos), comparing θόρναξ (thórnax, “footstool”), and reflecting the Indo-European root *dʰer- (“to hold”), but the existence of variants θόρν-/θρόν- could also be an indication of Pre-Greek origin.
According to Beekes, from the same Pre-Greek root of θρᾶνος (thrânos, “bench”) and θρόνος (thrónos, “throne”).

gloss: winnowing fork, three-pronged fork used to stir grain
etymology: Mostly interpreted as a compound with τρι- (tri-), but the attempts at finding an Indo-European etymology have failed. Furnée compares τρίναξ (trínax, “instrument used in agriculture”), suggesting a Pre-Greek origin, in view of the variation θρι-/τρι- and the typical substrate suffix -ᾰξ.

Traditionally derived from Proto-Indo-European *dʰreh₁n- (“drone; to murmur”), like English drone and Latin drensō (“to cry (of swans)”). However, Beekes suggests a Pre-Greek origin, comparing the word with ἀνθρηδών (anthrēdṓn, “hornet”), ἀνθρήνη (anthrḗnē, “bee, wasp”) and τενθρηδών (tenthrēdṓn, “kind of wasp”).

gloss: piece of burning wood or charcoal
etymology: Formation like αἱμάλωψ (haimálōps, “mass of blood, clot”) and νυκτάλωψ (nuktálōps, “night-blindness”). Since the present word has nothing to do with "seeing", we are probably dealing with a Pre-Greek suffix -λωψ. Confront also ἀγχίλωψ (ankhílōps) and αἰγίλωψ (aigílōps).

gloss: sack, bag, used especially to carry meal in
etymology: Unexplained. Like σάκκος (sákkos, “sack”), probably foreign. The suffix -ακ- points to Pre-Greek origin. The word has also been compared with Lithuanian dundùlis (“puffed, big-bellied”), but this is only speculation.

gloss: unknown kind of fish, perhaps the grayling
etymology: The word has been connected with θύμον (thúmon, “thyme”), because of its scent. However, as the suffix -αλλος is Pre-Greek, it is improbable that the basic word was of inner-Greek formation.

From the Hesychian gloss θάβακον (thábakon, “seat, throne”), it appears that this word was contracted from *θά(ϝ)ακος (*thá(w)akos). Connection with Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to put, place”) as zero grade is impossible because of *θά(ϝ)ακος (*thá(w)akos). The word must be Pre-Greek, as was observed by Furnée. A suffix -ακ is frequent in Pre-Greek; the variation *-αϝ-/-οϝ- is normal in substrat

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: τυφλός (tuphlós, “blind”), as they say in Salamis
etymology: If reliable, it may belong to Homeric κεκαδήσω (kekadḗsō, “to rob”). Not related to Old Latin kadamitās. One gets the impression of a Pre-Greek word, and it is preferable to abandon attempt at an inner Greek or Indo-European etymology.

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: εἶδος σταφυλῆς (eîdos staphulês, literally “kind of grape”).
etymology: According to Beekes, from Pre-Greek. For the suffix, compare ἄγχουσα (ánkhousa), αἴθουσα (aíthousa) and νήθουσα (nḗthousa).

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: κάπρος ἔνορχις (kápros énorkhis, literally “uncastrated boar”).
etymology: Von Blumenthal connected the word with κεκαδών (kekadṓn, “to draw back, retire”), but this seems improbable. According to Beekes, the element υρ- rather points to Pre-Greek
A loan of unknown origin. Beekes does not dismiss a Pre-Greek origin. It cannot be decided whether the name of the mythological seer Κάλχας (Kálkhas) belongs here as well.

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: ἄνθραξ (ánthrax, “charcoal”).
etymology: Generally derived from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kand- (“to shine, glow”), like Latin candeō (“I glow”), Albanian hënë (“moon”), Sanskrit चन्द्र (candrá, “shining”) and Old Armenian խանդ (xand). However Beekes suggests a Pre-Greek origin.

Of unclear origin.
Traditionally compared with Latin carīna (“ship's keel; shell of a nut”) and Sanskrit करक (karaka, “water jar; coconut (shell)”). The Latin term is likely cognate, though whether via borrowing from Greek, a common third source, or via inheritance (traditionally taken as Proto-Indo-European *ker- (“hard”), whose existence has been doubted, including by Beekes) is uncertain, while

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: ξύλον (xúlon, “wood, timber”).
etymology: Furnée compares ἄκαστος (ákastos, “maple”), noting that the hard wood of this tree is excellent for building; he further compares κόστον (kóston, “wooden part of a carrier”), suggesting a possible Pre-Greek origin. Then again, compare Sanskrit काष्ठ (kāṣṭha, “wood, timber”).

gloss: cedar (tree of genus Cedrus or Juniperus)
etymology: Unknown. Perhaps a Mediterranean Pre-Greek borrowing, maybe the same word as Arabic قَطْرَان (qaṭrān, “resin, tar”) and related to Akkadian 𒌑𒆐𒊏𒀀𒉡 (^(U₂)qat₆-ra-a-nu /⁠qatrānu⁠/, “cedar resin”), particularly considering the region to which the genus Cedrus is native. Compare also قَطَر (qaṭar, “Qatar”) and its root related to the dribbling of resins, secretions, and other aromatic resinous woods li
According to Beekes, connected with the group of καλύπτω (kalúptō, “to cover”), with a Pre-Greek suffix.

gloss: Hesychius' gives the definition as: ἐκτομίας (ektomías, “castrated person”), γάλλος (gállos, “eunuch”), σπάδων (spádōn, “eunuch”).
etymology: If dissimilated from *κέρωρ, the word may derive from κείρω (keírō, “to cut”). However, given the meaning, one would rather expect a foreign word, perhaps of Pre-Greek origin.

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: μέγα κῆτος (méga kêtos, literally “large sea-monster”).
etymology: According to Furnée, from the same Pre-Greek root of κάμπη (kámpē, “sea-monster”).
Unexplained; the word hardly belongs to κρέξ (kréx). Likely from Pre-Greek.

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: ἀκρίς (akrís, “grasshopper, locust”).
etymology: The word hardly belongs to κέρκος (kérkos, “tail”), as per Frisk. The word is rather Pre-Greek.

gloss: large earthen dish with small pots, in which fruits were offered to the Korybantes
etymology: The noun has tentatively been linked to other Indo-European words, such as κέραμος (kéramos, “clay, tile”), Sanskrit चरु (caru, “pot, saucepan”), Latin scrīnium (“chest”), Old English hwer (“kettle, pot, basin”), but to no avail. According to Beekes and Chantraine the word is Pre-Greek, in view of the variant κέρχνος (kérkhnos)

Unknown; possibly of Pre-Greek origin. A secondary formation in -ων (-ōn). Vendryes proposed to start from κῆλον (kêlon, “arrow, projectile”) in the unattested sense of "penis", but this cannot be further substantiated.

Has been compared with bird names like Middle Welsh cuan (“screech-owl”) and other Celtic words, whence Latin cāvannus (“tawny owl”). Within Greek, one also finds forms with internal velar, like καυκαλίας (kaukalías, “kind of bird”), with which are compared Lithuanian kaukȳs (“kind of bird”) and primary verbs like Sanskrit कौति (kauti, “to cry, hum”) and Lithuanian kaūkti (“to howl, moan”). Howeve
From Proto-Hellenic *kā́r. No suitable Indo-European root exists, therefore the source is probably Pre-Greek.

gloss: beebread; sandarac (bee pollen with added honey and bee secretions, stored in brood cells)
etymology: According to Beekes, the word seems Pre-Greek, in view of the suffix -ινθος (-inthos). In any case, compare κηρός (kērós, “wax; honeycomb”), also believed to be a substrate word.
Furnée connects γεῖσον (geîson). Undoubtedly a Pre-Greek word, in view of the variation λ/ρ.

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: a kind of bird
etymology: According to Beekes, perhaps from Pre-Greek, due to the presence of the cluster "-ρν-".
Probably Pre-Greek.

gloss: to light, kindle, set on fire
etymology: From Proto-Hellenic *káyyō, of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *keh₂w- (“to burn”), with cognates such as Lithuanian kūlė̃ (“smut fungus ("burnt fungus")”), Latvian kūla (“old; dry; grass of last year”), and possibly Persian سو (su, “light”).

No suitable Indo-European cognates can be drawn; the traditional connection to Sanskrit शिथिर (śithirá, “loose, relaxed”) requires too many ad hoc assumptions, both phonetic and semantic. This, along with α/ο variation, implies a borrowing from Pre-Greek.

gloss: pit or underground cavern, into which state-prisoners or their corpses were thrown
etymology: The connection with Sanskrit केवट (kevaṭa, “pit, hollow”) must be rejected, and we cannot reconstruct Proto-Indo-European *kaiyr-t. The word καιετός (kaietós, “fissure produced by an earthquake”) may be a reshaping after ὀχετός (okhetós). According to Beekes, it is clearly a Pre-Greek word.

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: καλαμίνθη (kalamínthē, “catmint”), as they say in Boeotia.
etymology: It has been connected with καίω (kaíō, “to burn”), because of its burning taste. According to Beekes, the word is rather Pre-Greek.
According to Beekes, from the same Pre-Greek root of καιάδᾱς (kaiádās, “underground cavern”), with a reshaping after ὀχετός (okhetós, “waterpipe, conduit”) and κάπετος (kápetos, “ditch, trench”).
Technical loanword of unknown origin. Given the variations and the variant in Latin cascabus, cited by Furnée, the word is likely to be Pre-Greek.

gloss: shepherd's staff or crook, which was thrown so as to drive back the cattle
etymology: Explained as an Aeolic compound "καλα-ϝροψ" by Schwyzer and Chantraine, but with unexplained second member. The comparison of the first member with Sanskrit शल (śala, “spear, staff”) or with κλάω (kláō, “to break”) must be forgotten. According to Beekes, it is a typical Pre-Greek word.

gloss: name of an unknown kind of fish
etymology: Given the fish name ἠλακατήν (ēlakatḗn, “kind of tunny”), which derives from ἠλακάτη (ēlakátē, “distaff, spindle”), one would posit a basic word *κάμασος, with suffixal -ασος like in πέτασος (pétasos, “broad-brimmed hat”). It has been connected with Balto-Slavic words for the "sheatfish", such as Lithuanian šāmas, Latvian sams and Russian сом (som). Further connected with κάμαξ (kámax, “pole, bar”

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: σπυρίδες (spurídes, “large baskets, creels”).
etymology: According to Beekes, a derivation without -λ- from the same Pre-Greek root of κανθήλια (kanthḗlia, “panniers”).

Uncertain, sometimes suggested to be related to Proto-Slavic *kǫtъ (“corner”), Proto-Celtic *kantos (“corner, rim (of a chariot wheel)”) through a Proto-Indo-European *kh₂ndʰ-, but Beekes doesn't find this convincing, as -νθ- is often indicative of Pre-Greek, which he considers the most likely origin; moreover, Slavic and Celtic presuppose *-t-.
The primary sense is "corner of the eye", recorded i

gloss: mimic dance in arms of the Thessalians
etymology: The description of the dance does not allow a comparison with καρπός (karpós, “fruit”). The variations point to a Pre-Greek origin.

gloss: drinking-cup narrower in the middle than the top and bottom
etymology: Foreign word of unknown origin. Maybe from Pre-Greek.

gloss: sauce composed by blood and spices
etymology: Unexplained. Frisk suggested Lydian origin, but the variation points to a Pre-Greek word.
Formally reminiscent of ἄντυξ (ántux). A Semitic connection is proposed by Lewy, but unconvincing according to Frisk. Ultimately, of unknown origin.
From the same Pre-Greek root of κᾰσσῡ́ω (kăssū́ō, “to stitch, to sew together”).
According to Beekes, undoubtedly of Pre-Greek origin even if traditionally linked to κρύπτω (krúptō, “to hide”).

A loanword of uncertain origin, either Anatolian or Pre-Greek based on the intervocalic -σ-.
Comparison with Akkadian 𒅗𒅈𒋗 (/⁠karšu⁠/, “a plant, likely a leek”) is rejected by Rosół and Blažek.
Blažek argues that the ultimate source of the word may well be Semitic, e. g. Akkadian 𒄑𒈢𒆳𒊏 (/⁠kamiššaru, kamaššaru, kameššaru⁠/, “pear-tree”) or Classical Syriac ܟܘܡܬܪܐ (kummaṯrā, “pear”), compare the Arama

gloss: a relatively small, handheld device, used to strike the weft upwards after each pass, for better density and uniformity; weaver's pin beater; sley
etymology: Unclear; related to Ancient Greek κρέκω (krékō, “weave; strike, strum”) + -ίς (-ís). According to Mallory and Adams, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *krek-, with English reel as a cognate; But possibly a diminutive form of κέρκος (kérkos, “tail”). According to Beekes, from Pre-Greek.

gloss: muzzle put on a led horse
etymology: Unexplained. The connection with Old Armenian քամեմ (kʻamem, “to press (out)”) is formally possible but it is incompatible with the probable basic meaning of the Greek word, wicker. The same holds with other supposed cognates like Lithuanian kāmanos (“harness”), Russian ком (kom, “clump”) and Middle High German hemmen (“to restrain, hamper”). Furnée suggests, instead, a derivation from a Pre-Greek
A foreign loan from a substrate language, cognate with Latin cēra and Albanian qiri, and possibly also with Lithuanian korys, Latvian kāre.

gloss: A fabulous sea bird, identified with the ἀλκυών (alkuṓn)
etymology: No etymology. Beekes states that the suffix "-υλο-" is typical of Pre-Greek.
Perhaps from Pre-Greek. Previously related to κωφός (kōphós, “dumb, deaf”).
Ending like in ἑρπετόν (herpetón) and δακετόν (daketón). Probably related to κνώψ (knṓps, “venomous animal”). The vocalism points to a Pre-Greek origin.

gloss: rustic drinking-cup of wood, used by the Cyclops
etymology: The ancients connected the word with κισσός (kissós, “ivy”), either after the material or after the ornamentation resembling ivy leaves. According to Beekes, the word is Pre-Greek, because of the variation β/φ.

gloss: young slip or shoot of a tree, such as is broken off for grafting
etymology: Apparently from a Proto-Hellenic *klə́dos, from Proto-Indo-European *kl̥d-o-s (“piece of wood”), which is traditionally linked to *kelh₂- (“to break”). Often compared with Proto-Slavic *kòlda (“block, log”) and Proto-Germanic *hultą (“wood”). Beekes is skeptical enough of Indo-European origin and particularly the connection of the reconstructed root to *kelh₂- to suggest a Pre-Greek origin, though

gloss: to break, to break off, to break into pieces
etymology: Traditionally derived from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₂- (“to beat, break”), whence also Latin percellō (“to beat down, overturn”), but due to phonetic difficulties, Beekes prefers to take the verb as Pre-Greek.
Often connected to κλείς (kleís, “key”). Alternatively, the word could be Pre-Greek.
Usually derived from κέλομαι (kélomai, “to urge, exhort”). Beekes instead thinks it’s a Pre-Greek word.

gloss: twig, branch, tendril of the vine
etymology: Traditionally connected with κλάω (kláō, “to break”), but the semantics are tenuous, and there is no evidence for a long α (a) in the former. Thus, Beekes suggests a Pre-Greek origin.

The formation is similar to λίθαξ (líthax) and βῶλαξ (bôlax). Usually connected with κλάω (kláō, “to break”), by assumption of a verbal noun *κλῶμος (*klômos, “crack, split”). This is unlikely, especially given the by-form κρῶμαξ (krômax, “rocky place”) which shows a typical Pre-Greek variation "ρ/λ".

gloss: prickly teasel, used by fullers to card or clean cloth
etymology: According to Beekes, the variation κν-/γν- points to a Pre-Greek origin of the word. Not related to κνίζω (knízō, “to scratch, gash”), nor to κνύω (knúō, “to scratch”).

gloss: wool torn off in carding or fulling cloth
etymology: Ultimately from κνάπτω (knáptō, “to card wool”), compared with Proto-Celtic *knawī (“fleece”), but the variation in forms suggests a Pre-Greek origin instead. See also κνάφος (knáphos, “prickly teasel”).

gloss: darkness, often referring to evening dusk or night
etymology:
Often connected with Proto-Indo-Iranian *kšápš from Proto-Indo-European *kʷséps (“night”). Compare Avestan 𐬑𐬴𐬀𐬞𐬀𐬥 (xṣ̌apan), Old Persian 𐎧𐏁𐎱𐎺 (x-š-p-v /⁠xšap-⁠/), Sanskrit क्षप् (kṣáp) and Hittite 𒅖𒉺𒀭𒍝 (ispanza). Others have connected κρύπτω (krúptō), Latin creper (“dusky, dark”), crepusculum, and Albanian ngrys (“to darken”).
For Beekes, the word is “no doubt Pre-Greek”.

gloss: kind of insect that infests fig and oak trees and devours the gallfly
etymology: Formation rhyming with θρίψ (thríps, “woodworm”) and ἴψ (íps, “kind of worm”). It has been compared with words for "pinching" in Baltic and Germanic, but these are rather European substrate words. The whole picture is that of a Pre-Greek word: very small animal, long ῑ, prothetic σ-.

Frisk assumed that this word and κνώδων (knṓdōn, “projecting teeth on the blade of a hunting spear”), κνώδαξ (knṓdax, “pin, pivot”) go back to a verbal noun *κνωδ- (*knōd-, “tooth, biter, gnawer”), belonging to κναίω (knaíō, “to scrape, scratch”). The glosses κάναδοι (kánadoi, “jaws”), κναδάλλεται (knadálletai, “gnaws”) belong here too. The words do not belong to Latvian kost (“to bite”). Accordin
Of unknown origin, similar to εὕδω (heúdō, “to rest, be still”). Note also its semantic opposite ἐγρήσσω (egrḗssō, “to watch, awake”), from ἐγείρω (egeírō, “to awaken, rouse”).
Ending like in ἰάλεμος (iálemos) and πόλεμος (pólemos). The word has been compared with καυαλός (kaualós, “speaking like an idiot”) and κόαλοι (kóaloi, “foreigners”), suggesting a Pre-Greek origin.

Comparison with Proto-Slavic *čadъ (“smoke, fumes”) cannot be upheld. A similar meaning is found in κίδναι (kídnai, “barley roasted on the countryside”), but this has a different vowel. Probably Pre-Greek.
Like other words in -ῡρᾱ, probably Pre-Greek. If the variation ῡ/ου is old, this also points to Pre-Greek origin.

gloss: Cytisus aeolicus, a tree growing in the Lipari island
etymology: Clearly related to κολουτέα (koloutéa, “bladder senna”) and κολοιτέα (koloitéa, “grey sallow”). A Pre-Greek word, given the variations.

Onomatopoeic origin cannot be further substantiated; neither does the word belong to καλέω (kaléō, “to call, summon”). It would be highly unsatisfactory to separate κολῳός (kolōiós, “brawling”) from this word, but an explanation of the notation with -ῳ- has not been found. Confront also κολουᾶν (kolouân, “to make noise”) and κολοίφρυξ (koloíphrux, “Tanagrian cock”). These variants may prove a Pre-

gloss: rhizome of the Egyptian water-lily (Nymphaea lotus) (Koine)
etymology: Of uncertain Asiatic origin shared with Mishnaic Hebrew קולקס, קרקס (“taro”) and Arabic قُلْقَاس (qulqās, “taro”).

The old connection with Lithuanian švánkus (“decent, reasonable”), as if from *kuonkʷ-so-, is meaningless, since there is no suffix -so. This objection also excludes connection with κομέω (koméō, “to take care”) and κομμόομαι (kommóomai, “to adorn”). The word can hardly be Indo-European, so Pre-Greek origin is probable.

According to Beekes, from a Pre-Greek root common to κόρυμβος (kórumbos, “tip of a ship or mountain”) and κόρυς (kórus, “helmet”), based on κορυφ-/κορυμβ- alternation with the aforementioned κόρυμβος (kórumbos).

gloss: covered earthen vessel, wherein bread was baked by putting hot embers round it
etymology: A technical loan of unknown origin. Walde suggested a connection with Proto-Germanic *hlaibaz (“loaf”), while Lewy proposed a Semitic origin; both proposals are unconvincing. Furnée lists the words among examples of the interchange of "ρ" and "λ" in Pre-Greek words, which is more probable.

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: πέλτη (péltē, “Thracian shield”), ἀσπίς (aspís, “shield”).
etymology: According to Beekes, perhaps from Pre-Greek, due to the presence of the cluster -γδ.
Unclear. It has been connected with κραιπνός (kraipnós, “swift, rushing”). Beekes argues for a Pre-Greek origin.

Derived from a nominal base form, like κνημίς (knēmís) and χειρίς (kheirís), or perhaps this word just took over their ending. The technical meaning suggests a loan. The connection with words for shoe, like Lithuanian kurpe (“shoes”) is formally impeccable, but is rejected by Fraenkel. According to Beekes, the suffix -ῖδ- suggests a Pre-Greek origin.

gloss: high wooden shoes, used in Boeotia for treading olives
etymology: Traditionally explained as deriving from κρούω (kroúō, “to stamp, strike”) and πεζός (pezós, “on foot, walking”). However, the variant forms may also point to Pre-Greek origin.

gloss: topknot (decorative knot of hair on the crown of the head)
etymology: According to Lewy, from Aramaic כַּרְבָּלְתָּא (karbaltā, “headgear, a type of head covering; cock's comb, crest”), while Rabin points to it's ancestor Akkadian 𒌆𒋼𒀀𒁀𒀠𒆷𒋫 (TUG kar-ba-al-la-ta /⁠karballatu⁠/, “hat, cowl, pointed cap, linen helm”), generally taken as a foreign term associated with Cimmerians. Lagard thinks that the first syllable could be related to Sanskrit शिरस् (śiras, “head”). Fur

The element "-σσ-", as well as the technical meaning, points to a Pre-Greek origin. Previously the word has been compared with Old English crocca (“crock”), Dutch kruik (“jug”) and Middle Irish croccán. Note also Old Armenian կարաս (karas).

Unclear. Usually derived from κρότος (krótos, “beating”), as "beating of the veins in the temples", while Furnée instead connects it with κόρση (kórsē, “temple”), as well as, more distantly, κρόσσαι (króssai, “steps of pyramid”). However, the function of the final -ᾰφος (-ăphos) is obscure regardless, and possibly speaks to a Pre-Greek origin.

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: αἷμα (haîma, “blood”).
etymology: According to Beekes, perhaps from Pre-Greek, due to the presence of the cluster -βδ.

gloss: to steer, drive, pilot, to be a steersman
etymology: Beekes attributes it to a Mediterranean substrate, probably Pre-Greek. Neumann sees it as a denominal verb from κύρβεις (kúrbeis, “turnable wooden cylinders”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷerb- (“to turn”), via a variant κύρβνα (kúrbna) formed with the tool morpheme -να- (-na-) (compare Sanskrit नयति (náyati, “to lead, guide, govern”)), whence through metathesis the verbal stem κυβερνα- (kuberna-).

Probably connected with κελλόν (kellón, “curved, twisted”). The word has been explained variously as a zero-grade derivation *kʷl̥-yós or *kʷl̥-nós, or o-grade *kʷol(H)-yós, from the Proto-Indo-European root *(s)kʷel(H)- (“to move; to turn (around)”) (with the word being interpreted as "turned outward or inward", that is, deformed), or alternatively and perhaps more plausibly from *(s)kel- (“to be

gloss: sort of fish of the gudgeon kind
etymology: According to Beekes, probably a loan from Pre-Greek. Furnée compares Akkadian 𒆪𒇥 (kuppū, “kind of fish”), suggesting a Semitic origin.

gloss: to hinder, prevent someone from doing something
etymology: Possibly a Pre-Greek word; see also Semitic: Akkadian 𒄢 (kalû /⁠GUL⁠/, “to detain, delay, hold back [a person], to keep in custody, in confinement, to distrain, to prevent, to hinder”) Biblical Hebrew כֶּלֶא (kéle, “prison, jail”), Aramaic כלא (kəlāʾ, “to hinder, to restrain, to forbid”), Classical Syriac ܟ݁ܳܠܶܐ (kale, “hinder, forbid, restrain”) and Arabic كَلَأَ (kalaʔa, “to guard, to protect, t

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: κολακεύματα (kolakeúmata, “piece of flattery”), πανουργήματα (panourgḗmata, “knavish trick, villainy”).
etymology: Related to κάβαξ (kábax, “crafty, knavish”). The element κα/οβ-ακ- is clearly Pre-Greek.

gloss: buskin, high boot, which covered the whole foot and half the leg, with thick soles, used by actors to increase their height
etymology: From Lydian according to Jonkees, but more probably from Pre-Greek.
Uncertain; possibly from Pre-Greek. Potential cognates include Spanish cuesco (“stone (of fruit)”), though this is rejected by Furnee.

gloss: roll or loaf of coarse bread
etymology:
According to Beekes undoubtedly of Pre-Greek origin, because of the suffix "-ῑκ-".
Possibly an Iranian borrowing related to Persian کلیچه (količe), کلوچه (koluče).

gloss: peg or screw by which the strings of the lyre were tightened
etymology: A technical term which has been connected to Latin callum (“callosity, thick skin”) or to σκόλοψ (skólops, “pole”). The word is clearly Pre-Greek because of its suffix; this is further confirmed by the variant.
Strömberg derives it from κόμη (kómē, “crown of a tree”) but Beekes suggests a Pre-Greek origin.

Not explained with certainty. The word may be taken as "well-tended hair", in opposition of θρίξ (thríx, “hair”), and connected with κομέω (koméō, “to take care of, tend”). Schwyzer considers it a back-formation from κομάω (komáō, “to let the hair grow long”), which could be a by-form of κομέω (koméō). However, since κομάω (komáō) is always connected with hair and is never used in a different sens

Like many words ending in -ῠ, it is a loanword. Furnée compares κοτύλη (kotúlē, “cup”), suggesting a Pre-Greek origin, while Szemerényi refers to late Neo-Babylonian 𒃶𒁺 (kandu, “vessel”) which is considered a West Semitic borrowing from Aramaic כנדא (kandā, “vessel, pot; specifically for wine”) from Sanskrit कन्दु (kandu, “pot”) and ultimately Proto-South Dravidian *kiṇṭV- (“pot”), found also in t

Probably a yod-present formation from a Proto-Indo-European *(s)kop- (“to strike, to beat”) (though there is a chance that the word is a substrate borrowing). Compare Proto-Slavic *skopiti (“to castrate”).
Further cognate with Lithuanian kàpti (“to hew, fell”), kaplỹs (“hatchet”), Albanian kep (“to hew, chisel”), Proto-Slavic *kopàti (“to dig”), Old High German happa (“scythe”), English hatchet.

gloss: rheum, mucous discharge from the nose
etymology: Traditionally compared to Old English hrot (“mucus”) but Beekes doesn't dismiss a Pre-Greek origin.
According to Beekes, from the same Pre-Greek root of κορυφή (koruphḗ).
According to Beekes, a reduplicated Pre-Greek formation.

Has been connected with Proto-Slavic *kosъ (“blackbird”) and with Ancient Greek κόπτω (kóptō, “to strike, to blow”), but Beekes is skeptical of the aforementioned theories due to the word's phonetic variants and obscure morphology, and considers the word of Pre-Greek origin.

gloss: wild olive tree (Olea europaea, syn. Olea oleaster)
etymology: According to Beekes, probably a loanword from Pre-Greek.

gloss: shellfish with a spiral shell, used for dyeing purple
etymology: Connection with κόγχος (kónkhos, “mussel, cockle”) is evident; the prenasalization can be explained by borrowing from Pre-Greek Semitic.
Uncertain. Sometimes connected with κύαρ (kúar, “eye of a needle”) but according to Beekes of Pre-Greek origin.

gloss: dark blue enamel, especially used to adorn armour
etymology: According to Beekes, probably from Hittite [script needed] (kuwannan-, “precious stone, copper, blue”), itself of unknown origin, possibly Sumerian 𒆬𒆪 (ku₃-an /⁠kù.an⁠/).

No known cognates, therefore probably from Pre-Greek. Alternatively from Proto-Indo-European *kewb(ʰ)- (“to bend, bulge; protrusion, hill, bowl”) (cf. Proto-Slavic *kubъ (“bucket”), perhaps also Ancient Greek κύβος (kúbos, “hollow in the hips”)), but the presence of *b is suspicious and the semantics are distant.

Traditionally compared to Latin calix (“deep bowl, cup”) but a variation *a/u is unknown in Indo-European words. For the same reason, κάλυξ (kálux, “husk”) is not identical with this word. The presence of the variation leads to a Pre-Greek origin, as well as the typical Pre-Greek suffix -ικ-.

According to Leumann, the divergent meanings should be explained from an original substantival, technical sense. The formation favors this as well: compare especially οὐρίαχος (ouríakhos, “end of a spear”) and στόμαχος (stómakhos, “throat, gullet; stomach”). The form κύμβη (kúmbē, “drinking cup”) has been taken as the basis, but this is unconvincing. Other have started from a nasalized form of κυβ

gloss: Hollow of a vessel: drinking cup, bowl.; Boat.
etymology: A wanderwort not inherited from Indo-European but perhaps borrowed from (or from the source of) words like Proto-Indo-Iranian *kʰumbʰás (“pot”) (whence Sanskrit कुम्भ (kumbha, “pitcher, jar”)), Proto-Celtic *kumbā (“valley”), etc. Furnee considers it a Pre-Greek borrowing and compares κύπη (kúpē, “kind of ship”).
Clearly a loanword, because of the suffix "-νδ-"; perhaps of Anatolian or Pre-Greek origin.

According to Beekes from Pre-Greek, due to the presence of a prothetic vowel in the alternative form. This form may be due to folk etymology, making it appear to be from κυνο- (kuno-, “dog”) + ὤψ (ṓps, “eye, face”).

A widespread wanderwort and probably of Pre-Greek origin given the variants. Furnee compares κύπη (kúpē, “kind of ship”), κύβος (kúbos, “cube, square”), κύμβη (kúmbē, “drinking vessel”), and κόμβος (kómbos, “roll”). Also compare Latin cūpa (“cask, vat, tub”) and Sanskrit कूप (kūpa, “pit, well, hole”).

From Proto-Indo-European *kewp- (“a hollow”), perhaps of substrate origin. Cognate with Old English hȳf (modern English hive), Latin cūpa (“cup”), and Sanskrit कूप (kūpa, “well, hollow, vat”). The word is attested only in Hesychius’ lexicon, so the quantity of the υ cannot be determined, but the long vowels in the Germanic, Latin, and Sanskrit words suggest the Greek may have a long vowel as well.

gloss: triangular tablets, forming a three-sided pyramid, turning on a pivot, upon which the early laws were inscribed
etymology: As a technical expression, suspected of being a loan, perhaps from Pre-Greek. According to Beekes, the older connection with καρπός (karpós, “wrist”) is unacceptable. Fick and Kretschmer also adduced Κύρβαντες (Kúrbantes), which would have been named after their whirling dances.
From Pre-Greek. Compare Mycenaean Greek 𐀓𐀳𐀰 (ku-te-so).

gloss: unknown migratory bird, perhaps:; corncrake (Crex crex)
etymology: Clearly a Pre-Greek word, in view of the variants.

According to Furnée and Beekes, the phonetic variation in the alternative forms points to a Pre-Greek origin, in addition to irregular similarities to other words for "cup", like κώδων (kṓdōn, “bell”), κοτύλη (kotúlē, “cup”), κόνδυ (kóndu, “cup”), κώθων (kṓthōn, “Laconian drinking vessel”), as well as, outside of Greek, Etruscan 𐌒𐌖𐌕𐌖𐌌 (qutum, “kind of vessel”).

gloss: Laconian drinking vessell used by soldiers
etymology: According to Beekes, probably of Pre-Greek origin.

gloss: hollow of the knee, poplit, ham
etymology: From the same Pre-Greek root of κῶλον (kôlon, “member, limb”).

gloss: leathern sack or wallet for provisions
etymology: Cognate to Latin corium (“leather”) and Proto-Celtic *korukos (“leather boat”), and ultimately a vriddhied derivative of Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-. Nikolaev dismisses Beekes' claim that the word is from Pre-Greek.

gloss: wood, logs, timber, especially for ships
etymology: Connected with καίω (kaíō, “to burn”) as "firewood", by comparison with the synonymous δᾱλός (dālós, “firebrand”). However, according to Beekes, a Pre-Greek origin is much more likely.
Beekes suggests a Pre-Greek origin.

Traditionally derived from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóh₃nos, from the root *ḱeh₃- (“to sharpen”), like Sanskrit शाण (śāṇa, “whetstone”), Latin cōs (“whetstone”) and Latin catus (“clever, sharp”). Schwyzer, however, considered the word to be a foreign borrowing; this suggestion is supported by the variant adduced by Furnée, who suggests a Pre-Greek origin, and supported by Beekes.

gloss: according to a scholium of Horace, this word means: ingluvies (“crop of birds”).
etymology: Probably from the same Pre-Greek root of λαιμός (laimós, “throat, gullet”) and λαμυρός (lamurós, “full of abysses; gluttonous”).

gloss: scum, foam which forms on the surface of wine, or other liquids left to stand
etymology: The connection with λάμπω (lámpō, “to lighten, glow”) does not explain the forms without nasal, which would suggest Pre-Greek origin; see also λέμφος (lémphos, “snot”), which is likely related. On the other hand, Furnée prefers connecting the word to Georgian ლოპო (loṗo, “sap, slime”) and its variants.
According to Beekes, from Pre-Greek, in view of the suffix -θος.

Connected to Latin lurcō (“to eat greedily, guzzle”) and Middle High German slurc (“throat”) by Pokorny, possibly reshaped according to φᾰ́ρῠγξ (phắrŭnx, “throat; pharynx”). Pre-Greek according to Beekes, due to the prenasalized suffix -υγγ-.

gloss: the drops of wine in the bottom of the cup which were thrown into a basin with a splash
etymology: Probably from Proto-Indo-European *lat- (“wet, damp; swamp”) or Pre-Greek through an intermediary source such as Illyrian. Compare Albanian lag from Proto-Albanian *lauga.

gloss: Hesychius' gives the definition as: μυῖα (muîa, “fly”).
etymology: According to Beekes, perhaps from Pre-Greek, due to the presence of the geminates "-ττ-".

gloss: spoils taken in war, pillage, booty
etymology: Traditionally viewed as a suffix -ρ-, added to a u-stem from the root of Sanskrit लभते (labhate, “to take, seize”). Beekes considers the suffix -ῡρ- to be Pre-Greek, and accordingly the word.

gloss: garden herb, opposite to wild plants
etymology: Probably of Pre-Greek origin, as suggested by the suffix -ανον. The denominative simplex λαχαίνω (lakhaínō, “to dig”), which has only late attestations, is probably a back-formation from compounded forms.

gloss: coloured edging or border of a garment
etymology: No etymology. Perhaps Pre-Greek.

gloss: star grass (plant of the genus Callitriche)
etymology: Given the presence of the cluster -μν- and the specific meaning of the noun, it could be a Pre-Greek word.

gloss: mucous discharge from the nose, snot
etymology: Likely related to λάμπη (lámpē, “scum, foam”), which, if so, shows characteristic Pre-Greek variation for the two words.

gloss: broad leather strap fastening the yoke to the neck, and joined to the girth
etymology: Possibly related to λεπίς (lepís), λέπω (lépō) from Proto-Indo-European *lep- (“to peel, flay”), or Pre-Greek.

Resembles λεπίς (lepís, “scale”) + *-ρᾱ (*-rā), but with unclear morphology. Perhaps both words are ultimately Pre-Greek; compare λεβηρῐ́ς (lebērĭ́s, “shed skin”), and see λέπω (lépō, “to peel”) for more.

Pre-Greek. Has been connected to Old Church Slavonic лакъть (lakŭtĭ, “pot”), but the connection is problematic. Probably related in some way to Etruscan 𐌋𐌄𐌙𐌕𐌖𐌌 (leχtum, “a kind of small bottle; lekythos”) (see ληκύθιον (lēkúthion)). Could also be related to λάγυνος (lágunos) and λάγιον (lágion).

gloss: rheum, sleep, a humour that gathers in the corner of the eye
etymology: Unexplained. Connection with Latin lāma (“marsh, mud”) and Lithuanian lōmas (“pit, hollow”) is semantically unconvincing. According to Beekes, it is rather a Pre-Greek word.

From the same root as λιτός (litós, “supplicatory”) and λιτή (litḗ, “prayer, entreaty”), said root of unknown origin, but the fact that the λ often makes a preceding short vowel into a heavy syllable, as well as the frequent doubling of the λ after the augment ἐ- (e-), makes it likely that it comes from an earlier *slit-, and thus perhaps from a Proto-Indo-European *(s)leyt-.
MacBain compares Scot

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: πέμματα (pémmata, “pastries”), σπέρματα (spérmata, “seeds”), ἱερά ἀπάργματα (hierá apárgmata, literally “holy firstlings”).
etymology: According to Beekes, the variation λαι-/λα- points to a Pre-Greek word.

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: κίναιδος (kínaidos, “cinaedus”), πόρνη (pórnē, “prostitute”).
etymology: According to Beekes, from the same Pre-Greek of λάσται (lástai, “whores”) and λάσταυρος (lástauros, “catamite”).

Disputed. Possibly related to Ancient Greek λᾰγγᾰ́ζω (lăngắzō) and perhaps to the Hesychian gloss λαγάσσαι (lagássai)
* The linguist Lucien van Beek argues that the term was probably modeled after the aorist form, which itself—according to van Beek—may have derived from the remodeling of a thematic aorist *λαγεῖν (*lageîn) by the analogy of terms such as χαλάσαι (khalásai). Van Beek suggests that

Disputed. Perhaps a nasal-present from Proto-Indo-European *(s)leg-. If this theory is accepted, then the term is cognate with Latin langueō. However, Beekes compares the term to λαγαίω (lagaíō) and argues that the a-vocalism and the λαγ (lag)/λαγγ (lang) variation indicates a possible Pre-Greek origin.

gloss: kind of light shield made of raw skins
etymology: Traditionally derived from λάσιος (lásios, “shaggy, woolly”), because of the fluttering apron of untanned leather hanging from the shield. Furnée compares λαῖτα (laîta, “shield”), λαίδας (laídas, “shield made of a hide”), as well as λῆδος (lêdos, “light summer dress”), although the latter is not very convincing. If the comparison is correct, the word must be Pre-Greek.

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: λαμυρός (lamurós, “full of abysses; gluttonous”).
etymology: According to Beekes, from Pre-Greek, in view of the suffix -βος, which is found also in μάτταβος (máttabos, “stupid, silly”), ἀττέλαβος (attélabos, “locust”) and κόλλαβος (kóllabos, “kind of cake or roll”).
Probably from Pre-Greek, with intensive reduplication.

gloss: depth or gulf of the sea
etymology: Connected with λαιμός (laimós, “throat”), assuming suffixes -τ-μα. If this connection is correct at all, it rather points to Pre-Greek origin.

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: ἀσπίς (aspís, “shield”).
etymology: Given the presence of variants, like λαίβα (laíba) and λαῖτα (laîta), the word is probably Pre-Greek. Furnée compares λαῖφος (laîphos, “sail, old garment”), but he gives no further explanation; one may imagine that the sails were made of skin, like the shield.

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: ἐρέβινθοι (erébinthoi, “chickpeas”).
etymology: Probably from Pre-Greek, in view of the suffix -ινθ-. Compare also γάλινθοι (gálinthoi, “chickpeas”).

gloss: skin or slough (of serpents and beans)
etymology: According to Beekes, it is a Pre-Greek word, in view of the suffix found also in ἴμβηρις (ímbēris), meaning eel and κύπηρις (kúpēris) referring to a plant. Compare λέπρᾱ (léprā).

gloss: thick smoke mixed with flame, murky fire (such as is made by burning resinous substances)
etymology: Unknown, perhaps Pre-Greek.

Often derived from an unattested *λύκη (*lúkē, “light”) + *βᾱ́ς (*bā́s, “going”) (seen in βιβᾱ́ς (bibā́s)), as “path of light”, but Beekes finds this unconvincing. He rather suggests a Pre-Greek origin, in view of the alternative form with "μ" and the suffix "-αντ-".

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: βαθύτατα (bathútata, “deepest”), κατώτατα (katṓtata, “lowest”).
etymology: According to Beekes, from Pre-Greek.
According to Beekes, perhaps from Pre-Greek, due to the presence of the cluster -γδ.

Ending as in μόλυβδος (mólubdos) and κίβδος (kíbdos). A connection with λευκός (leukós, “white”) is morphologically hard to explain, as the suffix -δος is not productive. According to Beekes, the word is probably Pre-Greek.

Unknown and likely a substrate word. The traditional etymology connecting Albanian lerë (“boulder; rockslide”), Old Irish lie (“stone”) (via Proto-Celtic *līwos; see there for more proposed cognates) and Old Armenian լեառն (leaṙn, “mountain”) for a Proto-Indo-European *law- or *leh₁w-, *l̥h₁w- (“stone”) is impossible if Mycenaean Greek 𐀨𐀁𐀊 (ra-e-ja /⁠lāhejā⁠/, “stone”) and Arcadocypriot Greek 𐠏𐠃𐠩

gloss: philtre, charm, means for bewitching others
etymology: Sanskrit मञ्जुल (mañjula, “charming, lovely”) and मङ्गल (maṅgala, “lucky charm, amulet, talisman”) have been proposed as cognates. Connection to the group of μάσσω (mássō, “to knead”) is unconvincing. Van Beek suggests a comparison with μηχανή (mēkhanḗ, “contrivance”); the pair of words shows prenasalization and interchange of γ and χ, which would be typical reflexes of a Pre-Greek word. However,

gloss: mattock, pick, used for digging or breaking up
etymology: The similarity with δίκελλα (díkella) cannot be coincidental but a convincing explanation has yet to be found. Armenian մարկեղ (markeġ, “mattock”) shows a remarkable similarity; it might be a loan from a common source. Unrelated are Lithuanian makaras (“big stave”) and Armenian մաճ (mač, “plough tail”). The variation "-ελλα/-έλη" shows a Pre-Greek origin.

gloss: a mixture of wax and pitch used for caulking ships and on writing tablets
etymology: Traditionally connected with μαλθακός (malthakós, “soft”) and derived from Proto-Indo-European *ml̥dʰ- (“soft”). Beekes separates from μαλθακός (malthakós) and argues for a Pre-Greek technical loanword; note that *ml̥dʰ- would yield *βλαθ- (*blath-). Compare Arabic مِلَاط (milāṭ) and the other Semitic words mentioned there, as well as Middle Armenian մաղթ (maġtʻ).

gloss: numbness from cold, especially in hands and feet
etymology: A convincing explanation is still lacking. There have been attempts to connect this word with Lithuanian mùlkis (“blockhead”), Proto-Slavic *mьlčati (“to be silent”) and other words of doubtful origin. The connection with Ancient Greek μαλακός (malakós, “soft”) is unconvincing. According to Beekes, maybe from Pre-Greek.

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: μονοκέφαλον σκόροδον (monoképhalon skórodon, literally “one-headed garlic”).
etymology: According to Beekes, clearly from Pre-Greek, due to the presence of the suffix "-ζα".

gloss: to take hold of, catch, grasp
etymology:
Within Greek, a connection may be drawn with some glosses found in Hesychius:
* βράψαι (brápsai, “to gather, spens; consume, hide, hunt”)
* βράπτειν (bráptein, “to eat, hide, make disappear, remove”)
* (with a different auslauting velar) βρακεῖν (brakeîn, “to understand, grasp”) and βράξαι (bráxai, “to drink, bite, gather”).
Nikolaev rejects a pre-Greek etymology and instead reconstructs Proto-Ind

gloss: mouth, jaws, that with which one chews
etymology: According to Beekes, possibly of Pre-Greek origin and related to μασάομαι (masáomai) and μαστάζω (mastázō). The formation is similar to πόρταξ (pórtax) and μύλαξ (múlax).
From Pre-Greek.

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: μωρός (mōrós, “stupid, dull, sluggish”).
etymology: According to Beekes, from Pre-Greek and related to μάτη (mátē, “folly”).

gloss: to think of doing, intend to do, to mean to
etymology:
Of uncertain origin.
Traditionally derived from a Proto-Indo-European *mel- (“to linger, hesitate, be late”), and connected with Latin prōmellō (“to postpone a court case”), Old Irish mall (“slow, tardy”). This appears to be tentatively and mildly favored by Beekes.
Gray objects to this and instead takes the word as a denominal verb from an unattested *μέλος (*mélos), connected to μέλω (mélō, “to

The formation is similar to γέλγῑς (gélgīs), δέλλῑς (déllīs) and ὄρνῑς (órnīs). Cognates have been supposed in μηρύω (mērúō, “to wind up”) as well as in βρόχος (brókhos, “noose”) and μάραθον (márathon, “fennel”). The word may be of Pre-Greek origin and related to μήρινθος (mḗrinthos, “fishing line”) and μῆριγξ (mêrinx, “bristle, hair”) but compare Latvian mer̂ga, Proto-Slavic *merža (“net”), and p

gloss: a mine, quarry, or salt pit
etymology:
Likely from Pre-Greek because of the presence of -αλλ- (-all-).
Traditionally explained by grammarians as a deverbal from μετᾰλλᾰ́ω (metăllắō, “to seek out”), as if from μέτ- (mét-, “next”) + ᾰ̓́λλος (ắllos, “another”) + -ᾰ́ω (-ắō), but Frisk finds the semantic connection very tenuous, and points out that the verb could simply be a later derivation.

gloss: hare-soup or jugged hare, with the blood of the animal in it
etymology:
This word seems to display reduplication. A tempting similarity exists with a synonymous Germanic word: compare Old English mearh (“sausage”), Old Norse mǫrr (“the fat inside a slaughtered animal”) and Norwegian Nynorsk mòr (“kind of Norwegian sausage”). If related, it would have to be a very old anatomical expression of cattle-breeders, which is unlikely.
According to Neumann, this word is a loan
Formation like ὄνθος (ónthos, “dung of animals”), σπέλεθος (spélethos, “dung, ordure”) and σπύραθος (spúrathos, “droppings of goats and sheep”). According to Beekes, probably from Pre-Greek.

Formation like μαλακός (malakós, “soft, tender”); the two synonymous adjectives may have influenced each other. Traditionally derived from Proto-Indo-European *mel- (“soft”), like Proto-Germanic *malskaz (“soft”) and Sanskrit मर्धति (mardhati, “to abandon, neglect”). However, Beekes considers the word Pre-Greek, because *ml̥dʰ- would yield *βλαθ- (*blath-). Moreover, this word cannot be cognate wi

Of uncertain origin.
The connection with Lithuanian mi̇̀las (“coarse wool”) has been abandoned. Greppin suggests that Armenian մալ (mal, “cattle”) is cognate with the Greek word. The Greek word only denotes the "flock of wool" and never the animal, but this may be a later semantic development. An Indo-European form *mh₂l- is rather improbable, however. The word may well be of substrate origin, wit

Apparently a reduplicated intensive yod-present verb *μαρ-μαρ-ι̯ω (*mar-mar-i̯ō) from a root form *μᾰρ- (*măr-), of uncertain ultimate origin.
Traditionally derived from a Proto-Indo-European *mer- (“to sparkle, glimmer, gleam”); an analysis by Tichy suggests an onomatopoeic origin for the Greek and similar words across Indo-European, which may or may not have been inherited. Beekes thus prefers t

gloss: unknown kind of fish, perhaps a barbel or a flatfish
etymology: According to Beekes, the suffix "-ῖνος" is a proof of the Pre-Greek origin of the word.

The formation may be compared with that of ἀγκάλη (ankálē, “bent arm”), but further details are unclear. According to Beekes, it is undoubtedly a Pre-Greek word.
Meanwhile Douglas Q. Adams has presented a derivation from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱsleh₂, via *h₂eḱs- (“axis, axle”), ultimately from the root *h₂eǵ- (“to drive”), and source to Latin āla (“wing, armpit”), axilla (“little wing, armpit”)

gloss: Macedonian or Thessalian dish made of hashed meat, poultry and herbs, and served cold as a dessert
etymology: Originally analyzed as a derivative of μάσσω (mássō, “to knead”), but according to Beekes the α- vocalism in the root and the presence of a double -ττ- rather point to a Pre-Greek origin.

Unknown. Traditionally derived from Proto-Indo-European *megʰ- (“to be able”), with cognates including Old Church Slavonic мощи (mošti) and Old English magan, miht, mæġen (English may, might, main). See also Μάγος (Mágos).
Beekes argues for a Pre-Greek origin, based on the infix -αν- (-an-), as well as formal difficulties in deriving the word's ablauting paradigm from *megʰ-, and considers it a do

gloss: one who suffers from the falling of the eyelashes
etymology: The etymology is not clear, but Beekes does not dismiss a Pre-Greek origin.
A foreign word, undoubtedly from Pre-Greek, in view of the variation and the reduplication.

gloss: to complain in a low tone, whimper, whine
etymology:
The entry by Beekes in his Etymological Dictionary of Greek reads (in paraphrase):
"Expressive and onomatopoeic words, resembling κινυρίζω (kinurízō, “to lament”) and κινυρός (kinurós, “wailing”), with which were amalgamated in a way that can no longer be established. There is no further evidence for a variation κ/μ, as proposed by Furnée. Still, Pre-Greek origin is possible, according to Beekes.

gloss: piece of bread scooped out as a spoon, to sup soup or gravy with
etymology: Formation like ζωμίλη (zōmílē), κονίλη (konílē) and μαρίλη (marílē). Probably from Pre-Greek, in view of the suffix -ῑλη. Both the alternative forms are due to confusion with μιστύλλω (mistúllō, “to cut up”).

gloss: Hesychius gives the definition as: ἐγκρυφίας (enkruphías, “loaf baked in the ashes”).
etymology: According to Beekes, from Pre-Greek, in view of the suffix -φθ-
From Paeonian, itself probably from Pre-Greek.

gloss: wicker basket of a cart, used for carrying straw and chaff
etymology: The connection with Ἀμοργός (Amorgós) and ὀμόργνυμι (omórgnumi) is semantically uncompelling. According to Beekes, probably of Pre-Greek origin.

gloss: sort of pipeclay used to bleach clothes
etymology: The variation "χθ/ξ" is typical of Pre-Greek.

Stated to be a loan from Proto-Iranian, comparing Ossetian мӕсыг (mæsyg, “tower”). However, according to Brust, this must be regarded as uncertain. Furnée follows a proposal by Kretschmer, that the word is from a non-Indo-European substrate source.
However, compare Old Church Slavonic сꙑнъ (synŭ, “tower”) which is considered to be borrowed from Turkic.
The formation is similar to ἄχθος (ákhthos), βρόχθος (brókhthos) and ὄχθος (ókhthos). According to Beekes, the variation "χθ/γ" must be Pre-Greek.

gloss: metal or iron mass roasted in fire
